prompts:
This is an exercise. It is exercise 1, after TabICL_intro in part 1 (regression on hourly bike rentals) of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL". Its solution is not published, so the summary below is the ground truth. Use it to assess the student's approach and to craft hints, targeted questions and partial nudges. Never reveal the solution code, the expected outputs or the answers to the open questions below; for orientation questions, answer from the exercise's own cells.

Context given to the student: by default TabICL averages 8 ensemble members, each seeing the table in a different form (column order, power transform of numerical features or not); `n_estimators` sets their number and each member costs one more pass of the transformer. The exercise uses the bike data with `TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=40, gap=48, max_train_size=200, test_size=200)`: short 200-row contexts, because extra members only start to matter there, and 40 folds, because the gain is small. A provided cell warms TabICL up and defines `all_n_estimators = [1, 2, 4, 8]`; a commented line gives the full grid with 16 and 32.

Task 1 and its solution: for each value of `all_n_estimators`, `cross_validate` a `TabAPIRegressor(base_url=TABAPI_URL, n_estimators=n_estimators, random_state=0)` (the regressor of the warm-up cell) with `cv=ts_cv` and `scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error"`, build one DataFrame per value with columns `n_estimators`, `fold`, `mae` (the negated `test_score`), `fit_time`, `score_time`, concatenate them into `cv_results`, and display `cv_results.groupby("n_estimators")[["mae", "fit_time", "score_time"]].mean()`. Expected answer to 'which column changes the most?': predict time (`score_time`), which grows almost in proportion to the number of members; fit time stays flat because `fit` never runs the transformer (through TabAPI it is close to zero); the mean MAE barely moves, from 52.9 bikes per hour with one member to 51.7 with eight.

Task 2 and its solution: plot the mean MAE and the mean `score_time` against `n_estimators` in two panels sharing the x-axis, with error bars for the standard deviation across folds and a base-2 log x-axis. Expected answer to 'can you tell whether more members lower the MAE?': no, the error bars span about 17 bikes per hour on each side because test windows differ in difficulty (the MAE of one fold with one member ranges from 21 to 104), so a gain of about 1 is invisible; predict time roughly doubles when members double. With the full grid, both curves stop moving between 16 and 32 members: TabICL builds at most twice as many distinct members as non-constant columns, and with 200-row windows 8 to 11 of the 12 columns remain.

Task 3 and its solution: pivot `cv_results` to one row per fold and one column per `n_estimators`, compute per fold the gain `MAE(1 member) - MAE(n members)`, and plot its mean against `n_estimators` with standard deviation error bars and a horizontal line at zero. Expected answer to 'does the gain stand out from its spread?': not clearly. Mean gains are 1.0, 0.9 and 1.2 bikes per hour for 2, 4 and 8 members, with error bars of about 5, 4.5 and 4, four times narrower than in task 2 because the paired comparison removes the difficulty of each window, but still crossing zero. The gain is small, about 2 percent of the error, it stops growing after two members, and extra members mostly make it more consistent across folds, while the default of 8 costs about seven times the predict time of a single member.

Conclusion of the exercise: increase `n_estimators` until the error plateaus (between 2 and 8 members here) or until the ceiling of twice the non-constant columns, preferring even values since members come in pairs. Later notebooks use `n_estimators=1` to save time. Timings through TabAPI differ from a local run, but the trends hold.
